title: Use mathematics to investigate and monitor the financial aspects of personal, business and national issues

lessons.title: Personal finance: budgets, payslips and debt
lessons.html:
Managing your own money

Good money management starts at home. A budget is a plan of income and expenses for a month.

Making a household budget

ItemAmount (R)
Net salary7 800
Rent2 200
Food2 500
Transport1 100
Electricity and airtime800
School costs400
Savings500
Total expenses7 500

Income minus expenses = 7 800 − 7 500 = R300 surplus. If expenses are higher than income, there is a deficit, and you need to cut costs or increase income.

Reading a payslip

Gross pay is your pay before deductions. Deductions may include PAYE income tax, UIF contributions, pension or provident fund, medical aid and union fees. Net pay = gross pay − deductions. Check your payslip each month: hours, overtime and deductions should be correct.

Interest and debt

Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount: I = P × r × t. Borrowing R5 000 at 20% per year for 2 years: 5 000 × 0.20 × 2 = R2 000 interest.

Compound interest is calculated on the amount plus interest already added. Saving R5 000 at 8% compounded yearly for 2 years: year 1 = 5 000 × 1.08 = R5 400; year 2 = 5 400 × 1.08 = R5 832. Compound interest makes savings grow faster, but also makes debt grow faster if you do not pay it off.

Before signing a credit agreement, check the interest rate, the monthly instalment, all fees and the total amount you will repay. Multiply the instalment by the number of months to see the true cost.

lessons.title: Business finance: costs, break-even and cash flow
lessons.html:
Monitoring the money in a business

Income statement basics

  • Revenue: income from sales.
  • Cost of sales: direct costs of producing what was sold, such as livestock purchases, packaging and direct labour.
  • Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales.
  • Operating expenses: overheads like admin salaries, insurance and rent.
  • Net profit = gross profit − operating expenses.

Break-even

Break-even is the point where income equals total costs, so there is no profit or loss.

Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (selling price per unit − variable cost per unit).

Example: a small poultry processing unit has fixed costs of R90 000 per month. It sells dressed birds at R60 and variable costs are R45 per bird. Contribution per bird = R15. Break-even = 90 000 ÷ 15 = 6 000 birds per month. Every bird above 6 000 adds R15 profit.

Cash flow

A business can be profitable on paper but run out of cash if customers pay late. A cash flow forecast lists expected cash in and cash out each month. If a retailer pays after 30 days but farmers must be paid on delivery, the business needs enough cash or an overdraft to bridge the gap.

Percentage change

Monitoring trends often uses percentage change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100. If monthly electricity rose from R40 000 to R46 000, the increase is 6 000 ÷ 40 000 × 100 = 15%.

Graphs to monitor performance

Plot monthly revenue, costs and profit on a line graph. A widening gap between revenue and cost lines shows growing profit; a narrowing gap is an early warning.

lessons.title: National issues: inflation, tax and exchange rates
lessons.html:
The economy affects us all

Inflation

Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. Stats SA measures it with the Consumer Price Index (CPI). If inflation is 5%, a basket of goods costing R1 000 last year costs about R1 050 this year. If your salary increase is less than inflation, your buying power falls even though you earn more rand.

Example: salary rises 4%, inflation is 6%. Your real income has fallen by roughly 2%.

Interest rates

The South African Reserve Bank sets the repo rate, which influences bank lending rates. When rates rise, loan and bond repayments rise, which affects both households and businesses such as farmers financing equipment.

Taxes

  • Income tax (PAYE): deducted from salaries based on SARS tax tables.
  • VAT: currently 15% on most goods and services, with some basic foods zero-rated.
  • Fuel levies: included in the fuel price and affect transport costs.

Taxes fund public services such as schools, clinics, roads and social grants. The national budget, announced each year by the Minister of Finance, shows how money is raised and spent.

Exchange rates

The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. If R18 = 1 US dollar and the rand weakens to R19, imported items such as fuel, fertiliser and machinery cost more, but exporters of products like citrus, wool or beef earn more rand per dollar.

Example: an export of 1 000 dollars earns R18 000 at R18 per dollar, but R19 000 at R19 per dollar.

Using maths to make decisions

Compare prices per kilogram, calculate true loan costs, check payslips, and follow inflation and interest rate news. These skills help you protect your household and contribute to sound business decisions.

Key points

  • A budget compares income and expenses; aim for a surplus.
  • Compound interest grows savings and debt faster than simple interest.
  • Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.
  • Profit is not the same as cash; monitor cash flow.
  • Inflation reduces buying power; exchange rates affect import costs and export earnings.
